newsitem.title: USA: Americans, Canadians need more calcium - U.S. panel.
newsitem.headline: Americans, Canadians need more calcium - U.S. panel.

text.p: Many Americans and Canadians need more calcium to keep their bones healthy, U.S. scientists reported on Wednesday as they unveiled new recommendations for this and four other key nutrients.

The daily dose of calcium, found in dairy products, some fish, tofu and broccoli, should range between 1,000 and 1,300 milligrams to help guard against the debilitating bone disease osteoporosis, an expert committee of the Institute of Medicine said in a report.

That is a significant increase over the 1989 recommendation of 800 to 1,200 milligrams made by the institute's parent, the National Academy of Sciences, which has set recommended daily allowances for essential nutrients since 1941.
Wednesday's report offered revised and expanded recommendations for calcium and four other substances linked to healthy bones: phosphorus, magnesium, vitamin D and fluoride.
The institute said in a statement that many Canadians and Americans do not consume the newly recommended amount of calcium.
The National Osteoporosis Foundation was encouraged by the institute's recommendation on calcium, saying the average adult gets between 500 and 700 milligrams of the nutrient each day.

Three servings of dairy products each day provide about 900 milligrams of calcium, and the rest of the requirement could be satisfied by eating canned salmon with bones, broccoli, tofu or calcium-fortified foods, the foundation said.
Calcium helps to prevent osteoporosis, which is characterized by brittle bones and fractures.
The institute's nutritional advice on calcium diverged widely from previous recommendations, and the report also vastly increased the amount of information included about each nutrient.

Where the old system set only the recommended daily allowance -- the minimum level of a nutrient needed to decrease the risk of chronic disease -- the new one will have that and three other categories, where data is available:
-- adequate intake, the goal for nutrition where no recommended dose is known;
-- estimated average requirement, the intake that satisfies the needs of half the individuals in a specific age group, and
-- tolerable upper intake level, which sets a maximum amount of a nutrient where excess intake could cause health problems.

"It is complex, but at least it's more scientifically sound than what it's been in the past," said Stephanie Atkinson of McMaster University in Hamilton, Canada, and a member of the institute's committee on dietary guidelines.

Atkinson said the new guidelines, which are broken down into recommendations for various age groups ranging from infancy through old age, are intended more for professionals than for the general public.
"Our mission was to set absolute values and then government and industry can use those values as they feel is most consumer friendly," Atkinson said in a telephone interview.
The institute plans future recommendations on folate and B vitamins, antioxidants, macronutrients, trace elements, electrolytes and water and other food components.
